breakfast.name: Mohinga (Fish Noodle Soup)
ingredients: Toasted chickpea flour (thickener — unique to Mohinga)
Banana stem (inner tender core — sliced thin)
Fried fritters (pe gyaw — split pea fritters), crispy shallots
instructions: Simmer catfish in water with lemongrass, shallots, ginger until cooked
Remove fish, flake the meat, discard bones
Strain and keep the broth
Fry a paste: shallots, garlic, lemongrass, shrimp paste in oil until fragrant
Add the catfish broth to the fried paste
Whisk toasted chickpea flour in water — add to soup to thicken
The chickpea flour thickening is Mohinga's unique texture technique
Add banana stem — it softens and absorbs the broth
Add fish back in
Boil noodles separately
Bowl: noodles, pour hot soup over
Garnish with hard-boiled egg, pe gyaw fritters, cilantro, lime, crispy shallots
Mohinga is Myanmar's national breakfast — eaten every morning by millions
breakfast.description: Myanmar's national dish and universal breakfast — rice noodles in a thick catfish broth flavored with lemongrass, shrimp paste, and a chickpea flour thickening that makes it uniquely Burmese. Every city, town, and village has mohinga vendors at dawn. The fritter-egg-lime garnish plate is the identity. No country eats fish noodle soup for breakfast the way Myanmar does.

breakfast.name: Mont Lin Ma Yar (Husband and Wife Pancakes)
ingredients: Quail eggs or small chicken eggs
instructions: The pan for mont lin ma yar is a cast iron mold pan with round wells
Heat pan, oil each well
Fill each well half with rice batter
Add a small cube of tofu
Crack a quail egg into the well
Top with spring onions, sesame seeds
Cover briefly — the steam finishes the egg
The batter sets on the bottom; the egg and tofu are cradled inside
They're called 'husband and wife' — each pancake has two components that fit together
Eat with fish sauce or soy dipping sauce
The round, egg-topped pancakes are one of Myanmar's most recognizable street breakfast images
breakfast.description: Myanmar's 'husband and wife' breakfast — small round rice batter pancakes with a cube of tofu and a quail egg embedded in each, cooked in a cast-iron mold pan. The name references the two components (batter + egg) fitting together. A ubiquitous street breakfast served at dawn. The visual of the cast-iron pan with many egg-topped rounds is iconically Myanmar.

breakfast.name: Nan Gyi Thohk (Thick Noodle Salad)
ingredients: Nan gyi noodles (thick, round rice noodles — like udon but rice)
instructions: Make a quick coconut-chicken curry: fry shallots-garlic-turmeric paste, add chicken, coconut milk
Cook until chicken is tender, shred
The sauce should be flavorful but not heavy — more of a dressing
Blanch nan gyi noodles — these thick, round rice noodles hold their shape
Toss while warm in toasted chickpea flour — the flour coats and adds earthiness
Add chicken, drizzle with curry sauce
Season with fish sauce
Garnish with hard-boiled egg, fried shallots, cilantro, lime
Nan gyi thohk is the 'salad' form of noodles — a dressed bowl, not a soup
The chickpea flour coating is the Burmese signature in noodle dishes
breakfast.description: Myanmar's thick noodle salad — round rice noodles tossed with toasted chickpea flour (creating an earthy coating), shredded coconut-milk-braised chicken, fish sauce, and garnishes. The 'toss' rather than 'soup' preparation distinguishes it from other Burmese noodle dishes. The chickpea flour coating is the Burmese noodle signature.

breakfast.name: Htamin Jin (Fermented Rice)
ingredients: Day-old cooked rice (fermented overnight — slightly sour)
instructions: Slightly ferment rice overnight — it becomes mildly sour
The fermentation is light — not strong — just a faint yogurt-like acidity
Massage toasted sesame seeds into the rice
Season with fish paste — the pungent, salty nga-pi is the flavor base
Toss with spring onions, fried shallots, oil
Serve at room temperature — this is not eaten warm
Squeeze lime — the acid brightens the fermented sour
Htamin jin is Myanmar's ancestral preserved food — before refrigeration, slightly fermenting rice preserved it
The result is lightly sour, sesame-rich, fish-paste-deep — complex from simple ingredients
Eaten as breakfast or as a component of the Burmese traditional meal
breakfast.description: Myanmar's ancestral fermented rice — day-old rice fermented overnight until mildly sour, tossed with toasted sesame, pungent fish paste (nga-pi), and fried shallots. The light fermentation is a preservation technique predating refrigeration. Eaten at room temperature, the sour-sesame-fish-paste combination is distinctly Burmese morning food.

lunch.name: Lahpet Thohk (Fermented Tea Leaf Salad)
ingredients: Lahpet (fermented tea leaves — the key ingredient, pickled for months)
instructions: Lahpet (fermented tea leaves) are the foundation — pickled for 6+ months, they're earthy, slightly bitter, tangy
The leaves must be washed and squeezed to remove excess brine
Assemble all the crunchy components: fried garlic, fried peas, sesame, peanuts, dried shrimp
The crunchy-textured elements are as important as the tea leaves
Toss tea leaves with the crunchy components
Add tomato, cabbage for freshness
Dress with fish sauce, lime, sesame oil
The balance: fermented earthiness (lahpet) + crunch + fresh + acid + fat
Lahpet thohk is Myanmar's most iconic dish — and completely unique
No other country in the world eats tea leaves as a food
The fermentation process creates a tea flavor profile that is food, not drink
lunch.description: Myanmar's unique contribution to world cuisine — fermented tea leaves (lahpet, pickled for months) tossed with a riot of crunchy components: fried garlic, peas, peanuts, sesame, and dried shrimp. No other cuisine eats tea leaves as a salad ingredient. The earthy, fermented tea flavor against the crunch is Myanmar's most distinctive food identity. Lahpet is so culturally central it appears at ceremonies.

lunch.name: Mohinga Kyaw (Dry Fried Mohinga)
instructions: This is the dry stir-fried version of mohinga — same flavors, no broth
Fry shallots, lemongrass paste in oil
Add flaked catfish
Add cooked noodles — toss with the fried paste
The noodles absorb the shrimp paste-fish sauce — they turn slightly golden
Add egg — scramble into the noodles
Season with fish sauce
Finish with bean sprouts (add crunch)
Spring onions, chili
The dry mohinga versus the soup mohinga — same cultural root, different textures
The stir-fried noodle method concentrates the flavors
lunch.description: Myanmar's dry-fried interpretation of the national dish — catfish, lemongrass paste, and shrimp paste tossed with rice noodles and egg in a hot pan. The broth is absent; the flavors concentrate. The same flavor profile as mohinga but eaten as a solid noodle rather than a soup. A lunch counter staple.

lunch.name: Shan Noodles (Shan Khauk Swe)
instructions: Braise chicken thighs in tomato with shallots, turmeric, soy sauce — low and slow
The tomato sauce should be thick and red-orange from turmeric
Shred chicken into the sauce
Cook flat rice noodles, rinse under cold water
The cold rinse stops cooking and keeps noodles from sticking
Serve noodles with the tomato-chicken spooned over
Drizzle sesame oil
Top with fried garlic, bean sprouts, pickled veg
Shan noodles come from the Shan State in eastern Myanmar — the hill tribes' food
The tomato-turmeric sauce is very different from the fish-paste mohinga base
The clean, bright, tomato-forward flavor is a contrast to coastal Myanmar food
lunch.description: Myanmar's Shan State noodle bowl — flat rice noodles with a bright tomato-turmeric chicken sauce, fried garlic, and sesame oil. From the Shan hill tribe region of eastern Myanmar, the tomato-forward, relatively mild flavor contrasts with the fish-paste-heavy coastal cuisine. Shan noodles are Myanmar's second-most recognized noodle dish after mohinga.

lunch.name: Nga Htamin (Fish and Rice)
ingredients: Freshwater fish (fried whole or in pieces)
instructions: The Burmese rice plate is deceptively simple
Cook rice — Burmese short-grain rice, slightly sticky
Fry whole small fish in oil until crispy
The crispy fish alongside rice is the central combination
Serve with ngapi on the side — the fermented shrimp paste is pungent and sharp
Ngapi is not for the uninitiated — intensely salty and funky
Fresh herbs, lime, chili alongside
Fried shallots over the rice
The 'traditional Burmese meal' is rice + fish + ngapi + whatever vegetables are available
The ngapi is optional but its presence is what makes the meal Burmese
Every Burmese family has their own ngapi source — buying it from specific vendors is a household tradition
lunch.description: Myanmar's most traditional meal — steamed rice with fried freshwater fish, a side of pungent fermented shrimp paste (ngapi), fried shallots, herbs, and lime. The ngapi is the Burmese food identity: intensely funky, salty, an acquired flavor that once acquired is irreplaceable. This simple combination has fed Myanmar for centuries.

dinner.name: Kyat Tha Hin (Burmese Chicken Curry)
ingredients: Onion (large amount — forms the sauce base)
instructions: The secret of Burmese curry: no coconut milk — the sauce is onion and oil
Fry very generous amount of onion slowly until golden and soft — 15-20 minutes
The onions melt into the oil creating the gravy base
Add garlic, ginger, turmeric, shrimp paste — fry the paste
Add chicken pieces, coat with the paste
Add tomatoes — they break down into the sauce
The long fry separates the oil from the onion-tomato — you see the red oil surfacing
This separation of oil is called 'si pyaw' — it means the curry is correctly cooked
Add water, braise until chicken is cooked through
Burmese curry is oilier than Indian, drier than Thai, no coconut richness
The separation of oil is the visual cue of a properly cooked Burmese curry
dinner.description: Myanmar's everyday curry — chicken braised in a sauce built entirely from slow-fried onions, garlic, and tomatoes without coconut milk. The defining technique is 'si pyaw' (oil separation): when the oil separates and surfaces red through the sauce, the curry is properly cooked. Oilier than Indian, drier than Thai, uniquely Burmese.

dinner.name: Hincho (Clear Vegetable Soup)
ingredients: Mixed vegetables: bottle gourd, drumsticks, spinach, or whatever is in season
Shrimp paste or fish sauce (small amount — just for depth)
instructions: Hincho is Myanmar's simple clear soup — the counterbalance to the oily curry
Fry garlic briefly
Add water
Add vegetables — heartier first (bottle gourd), leafy last (spinach)
Season with a small amount of fish sauce or shrimp paste — just a whisper
The flavor is very light — intentionally
Hincho is served alongside the oily curry and rice — the broth provides balance
The Burmese meal is a plate of rice + oily curry + clear soup + raw vegetables + ngapi
The clear soup is the 'refresher' element — no richness, just gentle vegetable broth
Seasonal vegetables mean hincho changes daily, weekly, with the market
dinner.description: Myanmar's gentle clear soup — a light broth with seasonal vegetables, a trace of fish sauce for depth, served alongside the rich oily curry. The hincho is the functional balance in the Burmese meal: the curry is oily and deep; the clear soup refreshes. The Burmese complete meal is always curry + clear soup + rice + raw vegetables.

dinner.name: Balachaung (Fried Prawn and Shrimp Paste)
instructions: Fry garlic in generous oil until golden and crispy — remove
Fry dried shrimp in the same oil until crispy
Add shrimp paste to the oil — fry it down until fragrant and darkened
Add dried chili, tamarind, fish sauce — balance sour-salty-spicy
Add back the crispy garlic and shrimp
Balachaung should be dry and crispy — not a sauce
The result is intensely savory, crunchy, preserved
Balachaung is Myanmar's condiment — a side that adds depth to any rice
It keeps well and has been Myanmar's traditional portable preserved food
Soldiers, traders, and travelers carried balachaung for shelf-stable flavor
One spoonful transforms plain rice into a complete meal
dinner.description: Myanmar's preserved condiment-side — dried shrimp and shrimp paste fried with garlic and chili until dry, crispy, and intensely savory. Balachaung keeps for weeks and historically served as portable sustenance for soldiers and travelers. A spoonful over plain rice makes a complete, satisfying meal. It's Myanmar's umami bomb in solid, crunchy form.

dinner.name: Ohn No Khauk Swe (Coconut Chicken Noodles)
ingredients: Egg noodles (wheat — the one Myanmar dish that uses wheat noodles)
instructions: Braise chicken with turmeric, shrimp paste, fish sauce until tender
Shred chicken into the cooking liquid
Add coconut milk — generous
Whisk chickpea flour in water — add to thicken (the Burmese chickpea flour trick again)
The result: thick, golden, coconut-rich broth
Cook egg noodles separately — these wheat noodles are the exception in rice-noodle Myanmar
Bowl: noodles, pour hot coconut chicken soup over
Garnish: hard-boiled egg, crispy fried noodles (crunch), shallots, lime, chili
Ohn no khauk swe is Myanmar's rich celebration noodle
The coconut milk + chickpea flour thickening is richer and more complex than a standard coconut soup
The crispy fried noodles on top — the crunch against the creamy soup — is the textural signature
dinner.description: Myanmar's coconut noodle soup — braised chicken in a rich coconut milk broth thickened with chickpea flour (giving a unique texture), served over egg noodles with crispy fried noodles on top. The chickpea flour thickening distinguishes this from any other coconut noodle soup in Southeast Asia. Often made for celebrations, the crispy-noodle-on-creamy-soup contrast is the defining bite.

dinner.name: Wet Thar Hin (Pork Belly Curry)
instructions: Same technique as Burmese chicken curry — the oil-onion base
Fry onion very slowly until deeply golden — the base for all Burmese curry
Add garlic, ginger, turmeric, shrimp paste — cook the paste
Add pork belly pieces — the fat from the pork belly will render into the curry
The pork fat merging with the frying oil creates a very rich gravy
Add tomato, water
Braise 45-50 minutes — the pork belly should be completely soft
The oil separation (si pyaw) should be pronounced — pork fat is added to the cooking fat
Serve over rice with fresh herbs, lime
Pork belly Burmese curry is the indulgent version — the pork fat enriches beyond chicken
Myanmar's Buddhist and Muslim communities approach pork differently; pork curry is most common in non-Muslim households
dinner.description: Myanmar's rich pork belly curry — slow-fried onion base with turmeric and shrimp paste, the pork belly's rendered fat merging with the cooking oil to create an intensely rich, deeply savory curry. The oil separation (si pyaw) is more pronounced with pork belly than any other meat. Served over rice — rich, oily, satisfying.

snacks.name: Pe Gyaw (Split Pea Fritters)
instructions: Soak split peas overnight — they soften but don't need to be cooked
Drain and blend coarsely — some peas whole, some broken
Add finely minced onion, garlic, ginger, turmeric, chili, salt
The mixture should be thick enough to form a spoonful
Drop spoonfuls into hot oil — fry until golden and crispy
Pe gyaw should be very crispy on the outside
They're the standard garnish for mohinga — but also eaten as standalone snacks
Pe gyaw vendors set up next to mohinga carts — the two are sold together
The split pea fritter is Myanmar's chickpea fritter equivalent
Turmeric makes them golden-yellow
snacks.description: Myanmar's yellow split pea fritter — soaked peas blended with onion and turmeric, dropped in hot oil until crispy. The essential garnish for mohinga (the national breakfast) but equally eaten as a standalone snack from street carts. The crispy split pea texture is Myanmar's most common street snack form.

snacks.name: Kyay Oh (Pork Offal Noodles)
ingredients: Pork offal: liver, intestines, blood tofu (optional — choose components)
instructions: Make a clear pork or chicken stock
Blanch offal components briefly in the stock
Offal choices depend on preference — liver is common; blood tofu is for the adventurous
Prepare rice noodles
Bowl: noodles, arranged offal, ladle clear hot stock over
The stock should be clear and clean-tasting — not heavy
Season at the table with fish sauce, white pepper
Add fried shallots, spring onion, garlic oil
Kyay oh is Myanmar's nose-to-tail noodle soup — practical and flavorful
The clear broth lets the offal flavors speak without being masked
A Rangoon street staple
snacks.description: Myanmar's offal noodle soup — rice noodles in a clear pork stock with liver, intestines, and blood tofu components. The clear broth is the point: unlike heavy coconut or spice-based broths, the clean stock lets the offal flavors come through directly. A Yangon street staple, practical and unapologetically nose-to-tail.

snacks.name: Shwe Yin Aye (Coconut Dessert Drink)
instructions: Cook sago pearls until translucent, chill in cold water
Cut grass jelly and agar into small squares — the color contrast is part of the presentation
Prepare palm sugar syrup — dissolve in water, chill
In a glass: add sago, grass jelly, agar, coconut strips
Pour cold coconut milk over
Add palm sugar syrup to taste
Top with crushed ice
Shwe yin aye is Myanmar's hot-season drink-dessert hybrid
Found everywhere in the hot dry season — street carts with colorful jellyboxes
The layered presentation of different textures in cold coconut milk is the visual signature
'Shwe yin aye' translates roughly to 'golden heart cool' — a cooling, sweet relief
snacks.description: Myanmar's hot-season dessert drink — cold coconut milk over sago pearls, grass jelly, colorful agar cubes, and coconut strips with palm sugar syrup. The layered textures in cold coconut milk is Myanmar's essential cooling street snack. Found on every hot-season street corner, the colorful jellybox display is unmistakably Burmese.

snacks.name: Sanwin Makin (Semolina Cake)
instructions: Mix semolina with coconut milk and sugar
Add butter or ghee, eggs — the eggs and fat give richness
Cardamom for fragrance — the warm spice is consistent in Burmese sweets
Pour into a buttered baking dish
Scatter poppy seeds on top
Bake until set and golden — the top should be slightly crispy
Cool completely before cutting — it firms as it cools
Sanwin makin is Myanmar's semolina cake — Indian semolina cake influence from colonial connections
The coconut milk replaces dairy milk — Southeast Asian adaptation
The poppy seed top and the golden semolina color are the visual markers
Cut into diamond shapes traditionally
snacks.description: Myanmar's semolina cake — semolina cooked with coconut milk, sugar, and eggs, baked until golden with poppy seeds on top. Indian semolina cake influence filtered through Myanmar's coconut milk tradition. The fragrant cardamom and the coconut richness make it distinctly Burmese rather than Indian. Cut in diamonds and served at celebrations and tea time.

desserts.name: Mont Lone Yay Paw (Glutinous Rice Balls)
ingredients: Palm sugar or jaggery (for filling — gooey center)
instructions: Mix glutinous rice flour with water into a firm but pliable dough
Pinch a piece, flatten into a disc
Place a small lump of palm sugar in the center
Seal and roll into a ball
The palm sugar melts when cooked — creates a gooey, sweet center
Boil the rice balls in water — they float when cooked through
Roll immediately in freshly grated coconut
The hot rice ball absorbs the coconut slightly
The contrast: chewy rice ball → molten palm sugar burst → fresh coconut exterior
Mont lone yay paw are Myanmar's water festival balls — made for Thingyan (New Year)
During Thingyan, families make these together in enormous quantities
desserts.description: Myanmar's Thingyan New Year rice balls — glutinous rice dough wrapped around palm sugar, boiled until the sugar melts into a gooey center, rolled in fresh coconut. The three-layer experience (chewy exterior, molten palm sugar burst, coconut coating) is the whole point. Made communally during the water festival, their preparation is as social as their eating.

desserts.name: Nga Pyaw Kyaw (Fried Banana)
instructions: Make a thin batter: rice flour, coconut milk, pinch of salt, optional sugar
Cut bananas lengthwise or in rounds
Dip banana in batter
Coat with sesame seeds — they stick to the wet batter
Fry in hot oil until batter is golden and crispy
The banana inside should be soft and sweet — the batter crispy outside
The sesame seeds add crunch and nutty flavor
Nga pyaw kyaw is Myanmar's most common dessert-snack
Sold alongside pe gyaw (split pea fritters) from the same vendors
The simple rice flour batter with coconut milk is the Burmese version of fried banana
desserts.description: Myanmar's everyday fried banana — ripe bananas in a coconut milk rice batter rolled in sesame seeds and fried until crispy-golden. The sesame seed exterior is the Burmese signature (contrasted with the plain batter in other Southeast Asian versions). Sold from the same street carts as pe gyaw fritters.

desserts.name: Mohkhinzar (Shredded Coconut Mochi)
instructions: Shred young coconut flesh — not the mature dry coconut
Mix young coconut with sugar and salt — simple filling
Make glutinous rice dough with coconut milk — the fat from coconut milk makes it tender
Pinch pieces, fill with coconut mixture, seal
Steam or boil
The dough is soft and slightly sticky when done
Roll in toasted sesame or desiccated coconut
Mohkhinzar is Myanmar's coconut sticky rice sweet — Burmese mochi
The young coconut filling is sweeter and lighter than mature coconut
The dough should be translucent at the edges when properly cooked
desserts.description: Myanmar's coconut mochi — glutinous rice dough made with coconut milk, filled with sweetened young coconut, cooked until the exterior becomes translucent and tender. The young coconut filling (lighter and sweeter than mature coconut) inside the chewy coconut-milk dough creates a double-coconut experience unique to Burmese sweets.

drinks.name: Lahpet Yay (Fermented Tea Leaf Tea)
ingredients: Fermented tea leaves (lahpet — the same tea leaf used in the salad)
Or: drink plain as a bitter, earthy tea
instructions: The same lahpet (fermented tea leaves) used in Myanmar's national salad can be made into tea
Steep lahpet leaves in hot water
The resulting tea is earthy, slightly bitter, deeply complex from the fermentation
Drunk plain or with sugar
In rural Myanmar, lahpet as a tea (not a salad) is the original preparation
The fermented tea tradition links Myanmar to the ancient tea-growing regions of Yunnan, China — they share a botanical border
Myanmar is one of the world's oldest tea cultures
The tea-as-food and tea-as-drink traditions exist simultaneously in Myanmar
This is the only country in the world with this dual tea identity
drinks.description: Myanmar's ancient tea drink — the same fermented tea leaves (lahpet) used in the national salad, steeped as a bitter, earthy, fermented tea. Myanmar sits at the origin point of tea cultivation (sharing a mountain border with Yunnan, China, the world's oldest tea region). The dual use of lahpet as both food and drink is Myanmar's unique tea identity.

drinks.name: Boh Boh Kyi (Ginger Tea)
instructions: Simmer fresh ginger slices in water for 10 minutes
The longer it simmers, the hotter and spicier it becomes
Add sugar — Myanmar's ginger tea is sweet, the sweetness balancing the ginger heat
Optional: add lemongrass for brightness, pandan for fragrance
Serve hot — the warming effect is the point
Ginger tea is Myanmar's cold and monsoon season drink
During the long wet season (May-October), hot ginger tea is everywhere
The generous ginger creates a warming heat that spreads through the chest
Myanmar's ginger tea is sweeter and simpler than Indian chai — no milk, no masala
The warming, sweet-spicy ginger cup is Myanmar's most comforting drink
drinks.description: Myanmar's warming monsoon drink — ginger sliced thick, simmered until the water is hot and spicy, sweetened generously. Drunk throughout Myanmar's wet season (May-October) as a warming, comforting cup. Simpler than Indian chai (no milk, no spice blend) — just ginger, water, and sugar. The intensity adjusts with simmer time.

drinks.name: Ye Nan Gya Kway (Iced Lime Tea)
instructions: Brew strong black tea — let it steep longer than usual
Cool to room temperature
Pour over crushed ice
Add fresh lime juice — generous — the sour lifts the tea
Add sugar syrup to taste
Optional: soda water for fizz
The combination: strong tea + sour lime + sweet sugar + ice
Myanmar's afternoon heat drink — consumed between noon and evening to refresh
The tea provides caffeine; the lime provides acid; the ice provides relief
Found at every tea shop (la phet yay zain — Myanmar's tea house culture)
Myanmar has a rich tea house culture — men gather for hours over tea and snacks
drinks.description: Myanmar's iced afternoon tea — strong black tea over ice with fresh lime juice and sugar. The tea house (la phet yay zain) is Myanmar's social institution: men (traditionally) gather for hours over tea and conversation. The iced lime tea is the hot-weather version. The tea house culture is as important to Myanmar society as the food itself.

drinks.name: Toddy Palm Wine
ingredients: Fresh toddy palm sap (tapped from the toddy palm tree at dawn)
Optional: ferment overnight for a low-alcohol version
instructions: Toddy palm sap is tapped from the cut flower stems at dawn — the fresh sap is collected
Fresh sap is naturally sweet and cloudy — a non-alcoholic health drink
Left to ferment for a day: mild alcohol develops
Left longer: strong palm wine develops
Myanmar's Mandalay region and dry zone have extensive toddy palm cultivation
The toddy palm tappers climb the 60-foot trees before sunrise to collect sap
The sweet, slightly yeasty toddy sap is drunk fresh in the morning
Myanmar's fresh toddy is one of Southeast Asia's most ancient beverages
Also boiled down to make Myanmar's jaggery (palm sugar) — so it's both sweetener and drink
The toddy palm tree provides: sap drink, palm sugar, and palm leaves for roofing
drinks.description: Myanmar's ancient palm wine — sap tapped from toddy palm trees at dawn, drunk fresh (sweet, non-alcoholic) or after a day of fermentation (mildly alcoholic). Myanmar's dry zone palm tappers climb 60-foot trees before sunrise. The same sap boiled down becomes jaggery (palm sugar), making the toddy palm one of Myanmar's most useful trees. One of Southeast Asia's oldest beverages.
